query: For as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles? Earlier work focused mainly on arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons, where an ordered single-phase hexagonal state undergoes a first-order magnetostructural transition that produces a large but sharp and hysteretic entropy change; these bulk forms also have limited heat-exchange rates because of their low surface-to-volume ratio. Prior searches have largely emphasized composition-dependent changes in transition temperature or response amplitude, with most studies pursuing only one optimization variable. Under the constraints of avoiding rare-earth elements, retaining mechanical stability and low cost, enabling rapid heat exchange, and limiting hysteretic losses, specify one controlled intervention that would distinguish the proposed governing explanation from alternatives, the predicted observations relative to the as-deposited baseline, the boundaries over which those predictions should hold, the prior observations that support the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing controlled nanoporosity via physical vapor deposition (sputtering) modifies the microstructure to enhance heat exchange and tune the magnetostructural transition, thereby reducing hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic cooling cycles.
generation.material_initial_state: as‐deposited, non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi‐type high-entropy alloy thin films fabricated by standard sputtering with relatively low nanoporosity
generation.intervention: fabricate samples using controlled deposition parameters (e.g., adjusted deposition rate and substrate temperature) to intentionally induce enhanced nanoporosity and an increased surface-to-volume ratio
generation.conditions: magnetocaloric testing under low-applied-field magnetic cooling cycles near the magnetostructural transition temperature, with film thicknesses typically between 100 nm and 1 µm
generation.structural_mediator: increased nanoporosity and higher interfacial area
generation.mechanism: The enhanced surface architecture improves the heat exchange rate by reducing thermal gradients and local stresses. This promotes a smoother magnetostructural transition, mitigating the abrupt entropy change and reducing hysteresis compared to less nanostructured films.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with engineered nanoporosity will show a broader yet less sharply peaked magnetocaloric response with reduced hysteresis losses and faster thermal equilibration relative to the baseline as‐deposited films.
generation.baseline: as‐deposited films with minimal nanoporosity produced via conventional sputtering
generation.boundary: the predicted behavior should be observable under low-applied-field conditions and near the magnetostructural transition temperature in thin films (100 nm–1 µm thick); effects may differ in bulk samples due to inherently lower surface-to-volume ratios
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative change in entropy and hysteresis reduction is uncertain and will depend on the extent and uniformity of the nanoporosity introduced. Further optimization and microstructural characterization are required.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloy thin films: one using conventional sputtering (minimal nanoporosity) and one using tailored deposition parameters to induce significant nanoporosity. Characterize the microstructure using TEM/AFM to confirm levels of porosity. Subject both sets to identical low-applied-field magnetic cooling cycles and measure magnetocaloric properties.
measurements: Magnetometry (hysteresis loop measurements) to assess changes in magnetocaloric response
Calorimetric measurements to determine the magnitude and width of the entropy change
Thermal response tests to evaluate heat exchange rates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoporosity-enhanced samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in hysteresis and improvement in heat exchange (i.e., showing no appreciable smoothing or broadening of the magnetocaloric transition compared to baseline films), then the hypothesis that the modified surface architecture governs the improved magnetocaloric response is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: While these studies demonstrate that the relationship between composition and phase stability in HEAs has certainly been considered, expansion beyond the circumstances around the σ-phase has been limited. The further inclusion of processing conditions—the importance of which has been emphasized earlier—to this equation beyond prolonged annealing has not been presented in the literature. Here, we propose a fabrication method applicable to both equiatomic and non-equiatomic HEAs, where controlled processing conditions determine the most probable and stable composition. This is demonstrated through a thorough experimental analysis that tests the following hypotheses: For HEAs, an equiatomic composition maximizes configurational entropy, but structure and phase stability are not necessarily optimized. CrMnFeCoNi is not the most stable or preferred alloy composition within the CrMnFeCoNiCu system if the processing conditions (especially a slow cooling rate from the melt) are controlled.

Delving deeper, unfortunately, RCP tends to overestimate the merits of the materials which have a large temperature range of magnetocaloric effect (δTFWHM) but small entropy changes [,] in no small part because materials with same relative cooling power can behave differently in a magnetic cooling simulation []. Moreover, one of the last printed books about magnetic cooling ignores this figure of merit []. In order to be of use in magnetic refrigeration applications the chosen materials have to show a large magnetocaloric effect—a large magnetic entropy change. Besides this, there is a list of requirements related with heat transfer, heat capacity, heat conductivity, chemical and mechanical stability, hysteresis losses, eddy currents losses, etc. Therefore, magnetic measurements can be a trusted guide in deciding if a material deserves the effort of complete characterization. Some compounds of the type A1−xBxMnO3 can be considered to be of interest for magnetic refrigeration because some of these compounds show −ΔSm values (−ΔSm ≈ 4–6 J·kg−1·K−1 for ΔH = 5 T) comparable to intermetallic alloys []. This is the case of our investigated compounds.

chosen.technique: physical vapor deposition (sputtering) with controlled deposition parameters to enhance nanoporosity
chosen.conditions: as‐deposited thin-film samples (100 nm–1 µm) measured under low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles near the magnetostructural transition temperature
chosen.why: This move most directly addresses the performance limitation stated in niche 2. By switching from bulk forms to a deposition process that yields a high surface-to-volume ratio, the experiment can test whether enhanced heat exchange (and consequent changes in the hysteresis and magnetocaloric response) is primarily governed by microstructural features associated with increased interfacial area. This approach, using standard thin-film fabrication and characterization techniques, clearly distinguishes the proposed mechanism from earlier work that emphasized only composition-dependent optimization.
